author: Claude (batch A9)
note: Uses, partners, deterrents, propagation and breeding (1.27.0)

data.summary: A shade-tolerant foliage plant grown for its patterned leaves; it has no safe practical uses.

uses.text: Bold patterned leaves for low-light rooms.
uses.caution: Contains calcium oxalate crystals: chewing it burns the mouth. Keep it away from pets and children, and wear gloves when cutting it. The common name "dumb cane" comes from the swelling it causes.

compost.why: Soft green leaves rot quickly. The oxalate crystals break down in the pile; wear gloves when chopping it.

partners_good.name: Aglaonema
partners_good.why: Same warm, bright-shade light and evenly moist soil, so they share a shelf or a big pot well.

partners_good.name: Peace lily
partners_good.why: Same shade and moisture; both like to be grouped for humidity.

partners_bad.name: Cacti and other succulents
partners_bad.why: They need full sun and dry soil between waterings, which this plant does not.

propagation.how: Cut a cane into pieces 2 to 3 inches long, each with a node, and lay them half-buried in moist mix. New shoots come from the nodes in 4 to 8 weeks.
Cut the top 6 inches off a leggy plant and root it in water or moist mix; the old stump sprouts again.

breeding.text: Aroids flower with a spathe; the female part is ready a day before the pollen is shed, so crossing needs two plants flowering a day or two apart, or stored pollen. Berries take months to ripen, and seedlings of named hybrids vary a lot. Dieffenbachia rarely flowers indoors.
breeding.patent: Many newer named varieties are patented (look for "PP" or "PPAF" on the tag). Propagating a patented plant is not allowed while the patent lasts, even for yourself.

data.summary: The edible fig: sweet fruit in summer, and hardy enough to live outdoors in Round Rock.

uses.text: The fruit is eaten fresh, dried or made into jam. Pick when soft and drooping; figs do not ripen after picking.
Grows into a large shrub or small tree in the ground.
uses.caution: The milky sap and leaves can cause a blistering rash in sunlight (phytophotodermatitis). Wear gloves and long sleeves when pruning.

compost.why: Leaves break down well; chop the large ones.

partners_good.name: Rosemary
partners_good.why: Same full sun and well-drained soil, so they share a dry, sunny bed or large pot.

partners_good.name: Comfrey
partners_good.why: Grown under fruit trees as a mulch plant; its deep roots bring up nutrients and its leaves feed the soil.

partners_bad.name: Lawn grass
partners_bad.why: Grass competes for water over the fig's shallow roots; keep a mulched circle instead.

attracts.why: Ripe fruit is eaten by mockingbirds and other birds; net it if you want the crop.

propagation.when: Late winter (January to February), while dormant
propagation.how: Cut pencil-thick pieces 8 to 10 inches long and stand them two-thirds deep in moist mix or garden soil. Most root by spring.
Bend a low branch to the ground, nick the bark, and pin it under soil. Cut it free once it has rooted, usually by autumn.

breeding.text: Common figs set fruit without pollination, and their seeds are not viable. Crossing figs needs the fig wasp, which does not live in Texas, so they cannot be bred at home.
breeding.patent: Some modern named figs are patented; older varieties such as Brown Turkey and Celeste are not.

data.summary: The mustang grape, a vigorous native vine with very tart fruit, used for jelly and shade.

uses.text: The grapes make tart jelly, juice and wine once well sweetened.
uses.caution: The juice can irritate bare hands; wear gloves when picking and crushing.

uses.text: Covers an arbor or fence in one or two summers.
Birds, foxes and raccoons eat the fruit.

compost.why: Leaves and soft prunings compost well. Keep out leaves with mildew or black rot.

partners_good.name: Clover
partners_good.why: A cover of clover between vines adds nitrogen and protects the soil; used in vineyards.

partners_good.name: Hyssop
partners_good.why: Said to bring pollinators and deter some pests near grapes.

partners_bad.name: Small shrubs and trees nearby
partners_bad.why: It climbs over and smothers whatever it can reach; give it its own support.

attracts.why: A favorite autumn food for many birds.

propagation.how: Take pieces with three or four buds, plant them with one bud above the soil, and keep them moist. Native grapes root readily.
Bury part of a long cane; it roots where it touches the soil.

breeding.text: Mustang grape crosses with other Vitis species. Breeders have used it for rootstocks that resist drought and the Pierce's disease that kills most grapes in Central Texas. Seedlings take 3 or more years to fruit.

data.summary: An annual morning glory with blue flowers, fast to cover a fence.

uses.text: Covers a fence or trellis in one summer.
uses.caution: The seeds are toxic if eaten. Keep them away from children and pets.

compost.why: The hard seeds survive most compost piles and come up wherever the compost goes.

partners_good.name: A fence or trellis
partners_good.why: Grow it on a support of its own.

partners_bad.name: Vegetable and flower beds
partners_bad.why: A serious farm weed: it twines over crops and smothers them, and self-sows heavily.

attracts.why: The morning flowers are visited by bees; hummingbirds visit sometimes.

propagation.when: After the last frost (late March in Round Rock)
propagation.how: Nick or soak the seeds overnight, then sow half an inch deep where they will grow. They do not like being moved.

breeding.text: It crosses with other morning glories of the same species group, but it self-pollinates so readily that seed usually comes true.

data.summary: The sweet potato; ornamental forms are grown for their leaves and trail from pots.

uses.text: Ornamental varieties do make edible tubers, but they are small and bland. The young leaves are eaten cooked as greens in many countries.
uses.caution: Only eat plants that have not been sprayed with garden chemicals.

uses.text: Covers bare ground or spills from pots quickly in summer heat.

compost.why: Stems and roots sprout again in a moist pile; let them dry out first.

partners_good.name: Coleus
partners_good.why: A classic container partner: same water, and the colors contrast.

partners_good.name: Petunia
partners_good.why: Same sun and water in a hanging basket or window box.

propagation.how: Cuttings root in water in about a week. Keep a few indoors over winter to plant out again in spring.
Store a tuber over winter in a cool dry place, then lay it in moist mix; each sprout ("slip") becomes a plant.

breeding.text: Sweet potatoes rarely set seed. Breeders cross them by hand in warm climates; seedlings vary a lot.
breeding.patent: Most ornamental sweet potato vines (such as the Sweet Caroline and Illusion series) are patented.

data.summary: A tough, drought-tolerant flowering shrub with yellow blooms from spring to fall.

uses.text: Long flowering season in heat and drought.
uses.caution: The seeds and pods are toxic if eaten.

compost.why: Leaves are fine; keep out the seed pods, which can sprout.

partners_good.name: Lantana
partners_good.why: Same full sun, heat and little water.

partners_good.name: Esperanza
partners_good.why: Same needs, and the two flower together all summer.

partners_bad.name: Thirsty plants
partners_bad.why: Frequent watering for them makes this shrub weak and leggy.

attracts.why: Nectar from spring to fall.
Visit the flowers.

propagation.how: Nick the hard seed coat or soak overnight, then sow half an inch deep in warm soil.
Possible but slow; seed is easier.

breeding.text: Crosses with other Caesalpinia and Erythrostemon are uncommon. Seed from a single plant is usually much like the parent.

data.summary: A thorny tropical vine with bright bracts; it flowers best when kept a little dry and pot-bound.

uses.text: Long seasons of color in full sun.
uses.caution: Thorns scratch; the sap irritates some people's skin.

uses.text: Planted where it can live outdoors, the thorny canes make a hedge people and animals avoid.
The bracts give pink to purple dye for fabric.

compost.why: Thorny canes break down slowly and are unpleasant to handle. The bracts and leaves are fine.

partners_good.name: Lantana
partners_good.why: Same heat, sun and dry soil.

partners_bad.name: Plants watered often
partners_bad.why: Frequent water means leaves instead of flowers.

deters.how: The thorns make it a barrier along fences.

attracts.why: Visit the small white flowers inside the bracts.

propagation.how: Take 6-inch pieces, dip in rooting hormone, and keep warm in a covered pot. They root in 4 to 8 weeks.
More reliable than cuttings for some varieties.

breeding.text: Bougainvillea seldom sets seed, and named colors come from chance seedlings and sports, not home crosses.
breeding.patent: Many newer named varieties are patented (look for "PP" or "PPAF" on the tag). Propagating a patented plant is not allowed while the patent lasts, even for yourself.

Self-heading types (such as Birkin and Black Cardinal) can be split where they have made new crowns or pups.

breeding.text: Aroids flower with a spathe; the female part is ready a day before the pollen is shed, so crossing needs two plants flowering a day or two apart, or stored pollen. Berries take months to ripen, and seedlings of named hybrids vary a lot. Philodendrons hybridize readily within the genus, which is how most of the named ones were made.

data.summary: Rosette succulents that grow in cool months and rest in summer heat.

uses.text: Sculptural rosettes for pots and dry gardens.

compost.why: The fleshy leaves are mostly water and can root in the pile. Chop them and let them dry for a few days first.

partners_good.name: Other succulents
partners_good.why: Same gritty soil and little water.

partners_bad.name: Ferns, calatheas and peace lilies
partners_bad.why: They want moist soil and shade; a pot that suits them rots a succulent.

propagation.when: Autumn to early spring (its growing season)
propagation.how: Cut a rosette with an inch or two of stem, let it dry for a few days, then set it on dry gritty mix. Water lightly once roots form.

breeding.text: Aeoniums cross easily with each other; many garden forms are hybrids. Each rosette dies after it flowers (the plant lives on through its branches), so let seed form on a flowering rosette if you want seedlings.

data.summary: Prickly pear: edible pads and fruit, very drought-hardy, and native to Texas in many forms.

uses.text: Young pads (nopales) and the ripe fruit (tunas) are eaten across Texas and Mexico, cooked or raw, once every spine and glochid is removed.
uses.caution: The tiny glochids lodge in skin; handle with tongs and thick gloves, and burn or scrape them off. Be sure of the species before eating it.

uses.text: Cochineal insects that live on prickly pear give carmine red dye, and the fruit gives a pink one.
Birds and many mammals eat the fruit.

compost.why: Spines and glochids survive composting and turn up in your hands later.

partners_good.name: Agave
partners_good.why: Same sun, heat and dry soil.

partners_bad.name: Ferns, calatheas and peace lilies
partners_bad.why: They want moist soil and shade; a pot that suits them rots a succulent.

deters.how: Planted along a boundary, it keeps out deer, dogs and trespassers.

attracts.why: The big spring flowers are worked heavily by native bees.

propagation.how: Twist off a pad, let the cut end dry for a week, then stand it one-third deep in dry gritty soil. It roots in a few weeks.
Slow; pads are much faster.

breeding.text: Prickly pears hybridize freely, which is why so many are hard to name.

data.summary: The medicine-cabinet aloe: soothing gel, easy pups, and very little water.

uses.text: The clear inner gel is a traditional soothing treatment for minor burns, sunburn and dry skin; some studies support it for minor burns.
uses.caution: Use only the clear gel. The yellow sap (latex) just under the skin is a strong laxative and irritates skin. Do not eat it. Toxic to dogs and cats.

Aloe leaves usually rot instead of rooting.

breeding.text: Aloe vera is mostly sterile and rarely sets seed. Other aloes cross with each other and with Gasteria, Haworthia and Astroloba (the hybrids are called ×Gasteraloe and similar).

data.summary: Roses: flowers for cutting and scent; floribundas and minis flower in flushes from spring to fall.

uses.caution: Never eat petals from roses treated with systemic insecticides.

breeding.patent: Queen of Elegance (WEKjucstokol) is a patented Weeks rose: propagating it by cuttings is not allowed while the patent lasts. Seedlings from it are yours.
